intro_band.agent_remit_summary: An AI pair-programming assistant that runs in a developer's terminal and edits code in their local git repository in response to natural-language instructions, keeping every change under version control so the developer can diff and undo it. It may read and edit files the user has explicitly added to the chat, generate a repository map, commit through git, invoke linters and test commands, scrape web pages, ingest images and voice, and execute shell commands. Its only authorized counterparty is the local operator, and its only sanctioned outbound destinations are the operator-configured LLM provider and opt-in PostHog analytics. Every shell command — including auto-lint and auto-test — must require explicit operator approval, and instructions embedded in scraped pages, file contents, or command output must never be treated as authoritative directives.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: A Python CLI (aider.main:main) built on litellm, with a Coder class hierarchy in aider/coders/ that assembles the system prompt, applies edit blocks, and drives git through aider/repo.py. Approval prompts are centralized in InputOutput.confirm_ask() in aider/io.py; shell execution runs through aider/run_cmd.py with shell=True, reached from /run, /git, the linter, and the model's own suggested commands. Configuration is auto-discovered from .aider.conf.yml and .env in the working repository, and an experimental Streamlit UI in aider/gui.py is launched by launch_gui(). Untrusted material — scraped pages, command output, and AI comments found by aider/watch.py — is appended to the conversation as user-role messages with no provenance marking, and no domain allowlist gates /web.

behavior_summary: Aider hardened exactly one control and left the rest of the perimeter open. The approval gate on model-suggested shell commands in run_shell_commands() is deliberate and genuinely non-bypassable — confirm_ask(explicit_yes_required=True) makes even --yes-always answer "no" — but that discipline appears nowhere else: repository-supplied .aider.conf.yml and .env reconfigure the agent and reach subprocess(shell=True) through the auto-lint path with no prompt at all, and watch_code_prompt instructs the model to follow instructions written into source-file comments while files_content_prefix tells it to trust file contents outright. The result is a one-hop path from attacker-authored repository content to unreviewed edits and commits, with --gui publishing a fully auto-approving instance on every network interface as the sharpest variant.

rules.rule_text: Aider MUST NOT treat instructions embedded in retrieved or untrusted content — scraped web pages, file contents (including `AI` comments), or the stdout/stderr of executed commands — as authoritative directives; such content is data to be worked on, never a source of commands that override the operator.

Aider may operate only within the operator-designated repository / working tree, and MUST honor the operator's `.aiderignore` / `--subtree-only` scope where set; any read, edit, or access outside this operator-configured scope is a trust-expansion finding.

Aider MUST NOT initiate code edits, git commits, or command execution in the absence of an explicit user instruction — a chat message, a triggering `AI!` / `AI?` comment, or an operator-supplied scripted message.
Approved Communication Channels
Experimental web UI; it MUST bind to loopback only and MUST NOT be exposed to a public or otherwise untrusted network.
Only operator-configured provider endpoint(s); connections MUST verify TLS certificates.
`/web` may fetch only from the operator-configured domain allowlist (closure); any other domain is a trust-expansion finding.
Trusted People / Accounts
Trusted Domains
Trusted Services / Integrations

Any outbound destination beyond the operator-configured LLM provider(s) and opt-in analytics is forbidden — see Trusted Domains (LLM-egress closure) and Forbidden Data Movement (repository-data movement).
Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)
Allowed Data Sources
Repository source, file contents, prompts, and credentials MUST NOT be transmitted to any destination other than the operator-configured LLM provider(s) required to perform the requested edits.
Analytics / PostHog telemetry is opt-in and OFF by default; aider MUST NOT send any analytics without explicit operator opt-in.
Analytics telemetry MUST NOT include source code, prompt/chat content, API keys or credentials, or personal information.
API keys and credentials MUST NOT be written into git commits, the repository map, or chat-history files.
Allowed Without Approval

All shell-command execution — `/run`, `/test`, auto-lint / auto-test, and any command originating from LLM output (a suggested command, or one implied by a triggering `AI` comment) — MUST require explicit operator approval before it is executed and MUST NOT run silently.
Editing or creating files that the user has NOT added to the chat MUST require confirmation before aider modifies them.
Adding externally fetched or command-produced output into the LLM context MUST require user confirmation.
Aider MUST NOT discard, overwrite, or bury the user's uncommitted work; any pre-existing uncommitted changes MUST be preserved (committed separately) before aider applies its own edits.
Aider MUST NOT rewrite or destroy git history; `/undo` MUST only revert a commit that aider itself created.
Aider MUST NOT bypass the repository's configured git pre-commit hooks unless the operator has explicitly authorized skipping them.

Aider MUST NOT run with blanket auto-approval (`--yes-always`, or scripted `--message` runs without a human in the loop) for destructive or code-executing actions; such actions are not authorized for non-interactive approval and MUST remain per-action.
If aider cannot commit its changes, or a git operation would risk losing the user's uncommitted work, it MUST stop and surface the condition to the operator rather than proceed.
When a command originating from LLM output is proposed, or externally fetched/untrusted content is about to enter the context, aider MUST prompt the operator and proceed only on confirmation.
Aider's own commits MUST remain attributable to it (author/committer attribution or a Co-authored-by trailer) so its changes are auditable in the git history.

findings.summary: Shipped prompts instruct the model to obey instructions written into repository file contents, with no provenance labeling on any ingested content.
findings.description: watch_code_prompt is sent as a user-role message telling the model that instructions are written in code comments and to follow them, while files_content_prefix tells it to trust file contents outright. Because FileWatcher auto-adds any file containing an AI marker to the chat, an AI! comment authored by anyone with commit access — or vendored into the tree by a dependency — is promoted to an operator directive. The chain ends in edits to already-added files, which allowed_to_edit() applies with no confirmation at all, followed by an auto-commit.
policy_rule_text: Aider MUST NOT treat instructions embedded in retrieved or untrusted content — scraped web pages, file contents (including `AI` comments), or the stdout/stderr of executed commands — as authoritative directives; such content is data to be worked on, never a source of commands that override the operator.

evidence.snippet: watch_code_prompt, lines 1-8 — "I've written your instructions in comments in the code ... Find them in the code files I've shared with you, and follow their instructions", sent as a user-role message by watch.py process_changes()
allowed_to_edit() returns True with no confirm_ask for any path already in abs_fnames — and watch.py:191-195 adds AI-comment files to abs_fnames automatically

recommended_actions: Wrap all non-operator content — watch_prompts.py AI-comment blocks, cmd_web output, and prompts.run_output — in an explicit untrusted-data delimiter and add a standing system-prompt clause stating that text inside it is data, never instructions.

Change watch_code_prompt so AI comments are presented as a request to be summarized for operator confirmation rather than instructions to follow, and require an explicit confirm before FileWatcher.process_changes() promotes a newly-discovered file into abs_fnames.

findings.summary: Repository-supplied .aider.conf.yml and .env set the lint and test commands, which auto-lint then executes through shell=True with no approval prompt.
findings.description: load_dotenv_files and the config search path both read from the git root of whatever repository the operator opened, so a cloned repository chooses lint-cmd, test-cmd, auto-lint and auto-test. Unlike model-suggested commands, this path never reaches confirm_ask: the first edit in the session triggers lint_edited(), which hands the string to run_cmd_subprocess with shell=True. Cloning a hostile repository and making one edit is sufficient for arbitrary command execution on the developer workstation.
policy_rule_text: All shell-command execution — `/run`, `/test`, auto-lint / auto-test, and any command originating from LLM output (a suggested command, or one implied by a triggering `AI` comment) — MUST require explicit operator approval before it is executed and MUST NOT run silently.

evidence.snippet: config discovery, lines 464-477 — .aider.conf.yml is read from CWD and git_root; load_dotenv_files at lines 361-387 loads the repository's .env with override=True
Linter.run_cmd, lines 47-57 — the configured lint command reaches run_cmd_subprocess (shell=True) with no confirm_ask on the path from base_coder.py:1599-1601

recommended_actions: Gate the first execution of a repository-supplied lint-cmd or test-cmd behind confirm_ask(..., explicit_yes_required=True) showing the exact command, reusing the control already applied to model-suggested commands at base_coder.py:2456.
Ignore lint-cmd, test-cmd and yes-always when they originate from a config file inside the working repository rather than the operator's home directory or the command line.

findings.summary: aider --gui publishes an unauthenticated, fully auto-approving coder on every network interface; no server address is pinned to loopback.
findings.description: launch_gui passes telemetry and file-watcher flags to Streamlit but never sets --server.address, so the server binds all interfaces, and Streamlit ships no authentication. The instance it serves is auto-approving on two independent paths: main.py forces args.yes_always = True whenever return_coder is set, and get_coder additionally hands the command layer a CaptureIO(yes=True). Any host that can reach the port can drive file edits and git commits in the developer's repository with no confirmation; only the explicit_yes_required shell gate still holds.
policy_rule_text: Experimental web UI; it MUST bind to loopback only and MUST NOT be exposed to a public or otherwise untrusted network.

evidence.snippet: launch_gui, lines 246-266 — st_args sets browser.gatherUsageStats, runner.magicEnabled, server.runOnSave and fileWatcherType but no --server.address, so Streamlit binds all interfaces unauthenticated
get_coder, lines 71-84 — CaptureIO(pretty=False, yes=True) is assigned to coder.commands.io, compounding main.py:546-547 which forces args.yes_always = True for the return_coder path

recommended_actions: Append --server.address=127.0.0.1 to st_args in launch_gui() so the experimental UI cannot be reached off-host, and add an explicit opt-in flag for any non-loopback bind.
Remove the unconditional yes=True from get_coder() in aider/gui.py and surface confirmations as Streamlit dialogs, so GUI sessions retain the same per-action approval model as the CLI.

findings.summary: allowed_to_edit() enforces neither repository-root containment nor .aiderignore, so model-supplied paths can escape the operator's declared scope.
findings.description: abs_root_path() joins the model's path onto the repo root and resolves it with no is_relative_to guard — unlike watch.py, which does check — so a path containing .. lands outside the working tree. On the same call, allowed_to_edit() consults only git_ignored_file(); the operator's .aiderignore spec is honored at add-time and in the repo map but never on the edit path. Both escapes fall through to a non-explicit confirmation that --yes-always and the GUI answer automatically.
policy_rule_text: Aider may operate only within the operator-designated repository / working tree, and MUST honor the operator's `.aiderignore` / `--subtree-only` scope where set; any read, edit, or access outside this operator-configured scope is a trust-expansion finding.

evidence.snippet: abs_root_path, lines 566-574 — Path(self.root) / path then utils.safe_abs_path (resolve only); no containment check, compare watch.py:95 which uses is_relative_to
allowed_to_edit checks self.repo.git_ignored_file(path) only; repo.ignored_file() (the .aiderignore spec) is never called on the edit path, only at base_coder.py:455 and commands.py:811

recommended_actions: In allowed_to_edit(), reject any path whose resolved form is not is_relative_to(self.root) before any confirmation is offered, mirroring the guard already present at watch.py:95.
Add a self.repo.ignored_file(path) check alongside the existing git_ignored_file() check at base_coder.py:2202 so .aiderignore and --subtree-only bind the model's edit path, not just file addition.

findings.summary: Every aider commit passes --no-verify by default, silently skipping the repository's configured pre-commit hooks without operator authorization.
findings.description: The --git-commit-verify flag exists but defaults to False, and GitRepo.commit() reads that default to append --no-verify. Hook suites routinely carry the checks that would catch what an LLM edit gets wrong — secret scanners, formatters, license headers — so the agent's commits are the only ones in the repository that escape them, and the operator is never asked.
policy_rule_text: Aider MUST NOT bypass the repository's configured git pre-commit hooks unless the operator has explicitly authorized skipping them.

evidence.snippet: --git-commit-verify declared at lines 491-496 with default=False and help text "Enable/disable git pre-commit hooks with --no-verify (default: False)"
if not self.git_commit_verify - cmd.append("--no-verify") — applied to every commit aider makes, including auto-commits of its own edits

recommended_actions: Flip the --git-commit-verify default to True in aider/args.py:494 so hooks run unless the operator explicitly opts out, and surface a one-line notice when the operator does disable them.
When a hook rejects an aider commit, report the hook output to the operator rather than falling back to a bypass.

findings.summary: --yes-always auto-approves every destructive file and git confirmation; only model-suggested shell commands carry the flag that resists it.
findings.description: confirm_ask returns "no" under --yes-always only when explicit_yes_required is set, and exactly one call site sets it. Everything else — creating a new file, editing a file the user never added to the chat, auto-fetching a URL found in input, folding command output into context, rewriting .gitignore — is answered yes without a human. Scripted --message --yes-always runs are a documented workflow, so this holds independently of the GUI exposure that also depends on it.
policy_rule_text: Editing or creating files that the user has NOT added to the chat MUST require confirmation before aider modifies them.

Aider MUST NOT run with blanket auto-approval (`--yes-always`, or scripted `--message` runs without a human in the loop) for destructive or code-executing actions; such actions are not authorized for non-interactive approval and MUST remain per-action.

evidence.snippet: confirm_ask, lines 866-867 — "if self.yes is True - res = 'n' if explicit_yes_required else 'y'"; the only explicit_yes_required=True call site in the subject scope is base_coder.py:2456
confirm_ask("Allow edits to file that has not been added to the chat?") at lines 2226-2231, and "Create new file?" at line 2207 — neither sets explicit_yes_required, so both auto-approve

recommended_actions: Set explicit_yes_required=True on the destructive confirmations in allowed_to_edit() — "Create new file?" and "Allow edits to file that has not been added to the chat?" — so --yes-always cannot widen the edit surface beyond the files the operator added.
Split the flag into --yes-always for informational prompts and a separate, explicitly-named option for destructive ones, so scripted runs cannot silently inherit both.

findings.summary: /web fetches any domain with no allowlist and appends the scraped page to the conversation as a user-role message with no confirmation.
findings.description: cmd_web takes the URL as given, scrapes it, and pushes the result straight into cur_messages as role="user". The remit's ingestion confirmation is honored for command output — both cmd_run and handle_shell_commands ask before sharing — but the web path has no equivalent gate and no domain restriction. check_for_urls does prompt for URLs it detects in operator input, but that prompt is not explicit_yes_required, so it auto-approves under --yes-always.
policy_rule_text: `/web` may fetch only from the operator-configured domain allowlist (closure); any other domain is a trust-expansion finding.
Adding externally fetched or command-produced output into the LLM context MUST require user confirmation.
When a command originating from LLM output is proposed, or externally fetched/untrusted content is about to enter the context, aider MUST prompt the operator and proceed only on confirmation.

evidence.snippet: cmd_web, lines 243-253 — scraper.scrape(url) result is appended to coder.cur_messages as role="user" with no allowlist check and no confirm_ask
check_for_urls, lines 972-977 — confirm_ask("Add URL to the chat?") without explicit_yes_required, so a URL embedded in an AI comment or pasted input is auto-fetched under --yes-always

recommended_actions: Add an operator-configurable domain allowlist consulted in cmd_web before scraper.scrape() runs, defaulting to prompting for any domain not previously approved in the session.
Add a confirmation before scraped content is appended to cur_messages in cmd_web, matching the "Add command output to the chat?" gate already used for shell output.

findings.summary: Runtime fetches to raw.githubusercontent.com and pypi.org are outbound destinations the remit never authorizes, and neither response is integrity-verified.
findings.description: ModelInfoManager pulls litellm's model-price and context-window JSON over plain HTTPS with no signature, hash, or pinned revision, and the result drives token budgeting and cost accounting for every session. check_version adds a second undeclared destination. No repository data leaves on either path, so the data-movement rules hold, but the counterparty and channel closures do not.
policy_rule_text: Any outbound destination beyond the operator-configured LLM provider(s) and opt-in analytics is forbidden — see Trusted Domains (LLM-egress closure) and Forbidden Data Movement (repository-data movement).

evidence.snippet: MODEL_INFO_URL set to raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/main/... and fetched at line 208 via requests.get(self.MODEL_INFO_URL, timeout=5, verify=self.verify_ssl) with no integrity check
response = requests.get("https://pypi.org/pypi/aider-chat/json") — a second outbound host absent from the remit's Trusted Domains

recommended_actions: Pin the litellm metadata fetch in aider/models.py to a specific commit SHA and verify a published hash before the cached JSON is used, falling back to the bundled copy on mismatch.
Document both hosts as expected egress and provide a single switch that disables all non-LLM network calls for operators running under egress restrictions.

findings.summary: PostHog is initialized with exception autocapture on, sending unredacted stack traces and exception messages that the telemetry content rules do not permit.
findings.description: Named analytics events are carefully bounded — properties are stringified and model names run through _redact_model_name — but enable_exception_autocapture=True opens a second, unbounded channel. Uncaught exception text carries absolute filesystem paths (including the OS username) and messages built from file or command content, none of which passes through the redaction the event path applies. The separate report_github_issue path shows the intended treatment: it reduces paths to basenames and asks first.
policy_rule_text: Analytics telemetry MUST NOT include source code, prompt/chat content, API keys or credentials, or personal information.

evidence.snippet: Posthog(..., enable_exception_autocapture=True, super_properties=self.get_system_info()) — autocaptured tracebacks bypass the _redact_model_name / stringify handling applied in event() at lines 213-240
exception_handler, lines 113-124 — the GitHub-issue path deliberately replaces full paths with basenames before showing the operator, a redaction the PostHog autocapture path does not perform

recommended_actions: Set enable_exception_autocapture=False in Analytics.enable(), or route autocaptured exceptions through the same basename-reduction used by report.exception_handler before they are sent.
Add a test asserting that no analytics payload contains an absolute path or the contents of a chat message, alongside the existing tests/basic/test_analytics.py coverage.

findings.summary: Chat and input history files record every prompt verbatim inside the working repository, with no redaction pass for credentials.
findings.description: append_chat_history writes user input, model replies, scraped page content and confirmation answers to .aider.chat.history.md exactly as typed, and add_to_input_history does the same for the input line. A provider key or token pasted into a prompt therefore lands in a plaintext file in the repository directory. The check_gitignore prompt keeps these files out of commits, but it is declinable and only fires when the pattern is not already ignored, so the on-disk exposure remains.
policy_rule_text: API keys and credentials MUST NOT be written into git commits, the repository map, or chat-history files.

evidence.snippet: append_chat_history, lines 1128-1136 — writes the supplied text to chat_history_file with no credential pattern scan or redaction step
check_gitignore, lines 189-192 — the .aider*/.env protection is offered via confirm_ask and can be declined or skipped with --no-gitignore, so it is advisory rather than enforced

recommended_actions: Add a credential-pattern redaction pass in append_chat_history and add_to_input_history that masks values matching common key formats before they are written to disk.
Create the history files with owner-only permissions (0600) in InputOutput.__init__ so a shared checkout does not expose prior sessions.

findings.summary: A failed pre-edit commit of the user's dirty files is logged but not treated as a halt condition, so aider still applies its edits over that work.
findings.description: The uncommitted-work safeguard is real — check_for_dirty_commit queues dirty files and dirty_commit commits them before edits are applied. But GitRepo.commit swallows any git error, prints it, and returns None, and prepare_to_edit discards dirty_commit()'s return value. When the protective commit fails — a locked index, a rejecting hook, a detached state — the edits proceed anyway, and the escalation rule's halt never fires.
policy_rule_text: If aider cannot commit its changes, or a git operation would risk losing the user's uncommitted work, it MUST stop and surface the condition to the operator rather than proceed.

evidence.snippet: except ANY_GIT_ERROR as err - self.io.tool_error(f"Unable to commit: {err}") with the trailing comment "No return here, implicitly returns None" — the failure is reported but not raised
prepare_to_edit calls self.dirty_commit() at line 2291 and ignores the result, returning the edit list unconditionally at line 2294

recommended_actions: Have prepare_to_edit check dirty_commit()'s return value and abandon the edit batch with an operator-facing error when the protective commit did not succeed.
Distinguish "nothing to commit" from "commit failed" in GitRepo.commit so the caller can tell a no-op from a lost safeguard.

findings.summary: The only always-on record is a free-form Markdown transcript with no timestamps, so shell executions and file writes leave no machine-readable audit trail.
findings.description: Confirmation prompts and their answers do reach .aider.chat.history.md, which is more than many agents record, but the format is prose with no schema, no per-entry time, and no action type. The two structured sinks that would support detection — --llm-history-file and --analytics-log — are both off unless the operator names a path.

evidence.snippet: append_chat_history writes blockquoted Markdown to chat_history_file; no timestamp, event type, or file-path field is emitted alongside the text
--llm-history-file declared with default=None, and --analytics-log likewise unset by default, so no structured record exists unless the operator opts in

recommended_actions: Emit a JSON-lines action log alongside the Markdown transcript recording, per event, a UTC timestamp, the action type (edit, commit, shell, web-fetch), the target path or command, and the approval decision returned by confirm_ask.
Record the outcome of every run_cmd and lint_edited invocation to that log, including the auto-lint path that currently produces no record at all.

positives.title: Non-bypassable approval gate on model-suggested shell commands
positives.description: Commands the model proposes are confirmed with explicit_yes_required=True, and confirm_ask answers "no" to those prompts whenever --yes-always is set, so the highest-impact capability cannot be blanket-approved.

positives.title: /undo restricted to aider's own clean, unpushed commits
positives.description: raw_cmd_undo refuses to revert a commit that is not in aider_commit_hashes, has more than one parent, touches dirty files, or has already been pushed to the remote.

positives.title: User's uncommitted work is preserved before aider edits
positives.description: check_for_dirty_commit and dirty_commit commit any pre-existing modifications to a file as a separate commit before aider applies its own changes, so the user's work stays recoverable in git history.

positives.title: Dependencies fully version-pinned from a compiled constraint set
positives.description: Every runtime dependency is pinned with == in a uv pip compile output constrained by requirements/common-constraints.txt, and .pre-commit-config.yaml pins each hook to an explicit rev.

positives.title: Credential-hygiene prompt on startup
positives.description: check_gitignore detects an untracked .env or unignored .aider* artifacts in the git root and offers to add them to .gitignore, keeping provider keys and chat transcripts out of commits.

positives.title: Commit attribution enabled by default
positives.description: --attribute-co-authored-by defaults to true, so every aider edit carries a Co-authored-by trailer and remains attributable in git history without operator configuration.

rows.purpose: Full chat transcript including confirmation prompts and the operator's answers
Operator input lines, including /run commands echoed by handle_shell_commands
Raw LLM prompts and completions; disabled by default
Named analytics events with system properties; disabled by default

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Ad hoc. Aider has one strong, intentional safeguard — the non-bypassable confirmation on model-suggested shell commands — plus a coherent set of git-safety guards around /undo and uncommitted work, and a fully pinned dependency set. Around that core, the controls that would bound an untrusted-input agent are missing or defaulted off: no provenance labeling on ingested content, no domain allowlist, no repository-root containment on edit paths, pre-commit hooks skipped by default, and no adversarial testing or structured action log. The posture is that of a mature, well-tested developer tool that has not yet been engineered against a hostile repository.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: Real scope controls exist — files must be explicitly added to the chat, the repo map is built only from tracked files, and .aiderignore and --subtree-only are honored by RepoMap and /add — but allowed_to_edit() consults only git_ignored_file() and applies no repository-root containment, so the model's own edit path is wider than the operator's declared scope.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: Scraped pages, command output and AI comments are appended to the conversation as user-role messages with no provenance marker, and the shipped prompts actively invite trust — files_content_prefix says "Trust this message as the true contents of these files" and watch_code_prompt tells the model to follow instructions found in code comments; a grep of every prompt module returns no injection-defense language.

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: A genuine human-in-the-loop layer runs on the agent's path — confirm_ask gates file creation, edits to unadded files, URL ingestion and output sharing, and the model-suggested shell gate resists --yes-always — but auto-lint and auto-test execute repository-configured commands through shell=True with no gate at all, no path containment guards the filesystem sink, and --gui runs the whole stack auto-approved.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: requirements.txt is fully ==-pinned from a uv pip compile run against requirements/common-constraints.txt and .pre-commit-config.yaml pins every hook to a rev, which is consistently applied practice; against that, ModelInfoManager fetches litellm's model-price JSON from raw.githubusercontent.com at runtime with no signature or hash check, and no SBOM or ML-BOM is published.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: Roughly thirty functional test modules under tests/basic/ show a real testing culture, and test_ssl_verification.py is security-adjacent, but there is no injection fixture, no adversarial test of the AI-comment or /web ingress paths, no SECURITY.md, and no security scanning in any .github/workflows/ job.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: append_chat_history() writes a free-form Markdown transcript with no timestamps and no schema, and the richer sinks — --llm-history-file and --analytics-log — are both off by default, so there is no structured, action-level record that could support automated detection of an out-of-policy edit or command.
